title: Danville and Constitution Square
summary: Kentucky's road to statehood ran through a three-acre square in Danville, on land John Crow deeded in 1784 to Walker Daniel, the town's namesake.
bodyMarkdown:
Kentucky's road to statehood ran through a three-acre square in [Danville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Danville,_Kentucky). Its story begins at Fort Harrod, built in 1774 by settlers led by James Harrod. Three of those settlers, Thomas Harrod, John Crow and James Brown, soon claimed land around present-day Danville.

In 1784, Crow deeded 76 acres to [Walker Daniel](/stories/walker-daniel-danvilles-namesake/), the town's namesake, to form the town. The public square was set near the eastern end of the plot, not at the center as was usual. According to the history of [Constitution Square](https://grokipedia.com/page/constitution_square_historic_site), the spot lay about 500 feet from Crow's Station and gave an escape route in case of Indian attack.

## A court on the frontier

That fear reflected a real war. In 1780, for example, Shawnee, Odawa and Ojibwe warriors joined a British force that [captured two Kentucky stations](/stories/ojibwe-on-birds-war-road/), fighting the settlement of lands they claimed. Their leaders included [Blue Jacket](/stories/blue-jacket-weyapiersenwah/).

The Virginia General Assembly created the Judicial District of Kentucky in 1783. Harrodsburg was the first seat, but its facilities were poor, so the district's supreme court moved its next session to Crow's Station and ordered a courthouse built. The courthouse went up on the square in March 1785, and the court met there until statehood in 1792.

## Ten conventions

Between 1784 and 1792, ten conventions met in Danville to work out separation from Virginia. Grokipedia's Danville article says the delegates dealt with separation, navigation rights on the Mississippi River and protection against Native raids. The square's own history counts the conventions from 1785, the year the courthouse opened, so the start date varies by source.

The tenth convention met from April 2 to April 19, 1792. Five delegates from each of Kentucky's nine counties drafted and adopted the first state constitution. Congress had approved statehood on February 4, 1792, and Kentucky joined the Union on June 1, 1792. [George Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nicholas_(politician)), who helped write that constitution, is remembered in the name of [Nicholasville](/stories/nicholasville-takes-shape/).

## After statehood

The square fell out of use once the district court ended. The trustees sold it off in pieces beginning in 1817. During the Civil War, its brick courthouse, then part of a seminary, served as a hospital for wounded Union and Confederate soldiers after the Battle of Perryville.

## Kentucky today

The square was a state park from 1937 to 2012 and was handed to Boyle County on March 6, 2012. It was listed as a historic district on the National Register of Historic Places on April 2, 1976. It now holds replicas of three buildings and an original post office described as the first west of the Alleghenies.
